items.reason: 'feels the heralding foreboding of that stifling hour when the whale shall hold him' — 'heralding foreboding' stacks two near-synonyms and trips aloud; 'shall' is leftover archaic future in the preacher's narration.
items.new: "Now Jonah's Captain, shipmates, was one whose discernment detects crime in anyone, but whose greed exposes it only in the penniless. In this world, shipmates, sin that pays its way can travel freely, and without a passport; whereas Virtue, if a pauper, is stopped at every frontier. So Jonah's Captain gets ready to test the length of Jonah's purse before he judges him openly. He charges him three times the usual sum; and Jonah agrees to it. Then the Captain knows that Jonah is a fugitive; but at the same time he resolves to help a flight that paves its trail with gold. Yet when Jonah actually takes out his purse, prudent suspicions still trouble the Captain. He rings every coin to find a counterfeit. 'Not a forger, anyway,' he mutters; and Jonah is entered for his passage. 'Show me my stateroom, sir,' says Jonah now; 'I'm travel-weary; I need sleep.' 'You look it,' says the Captain; 'there's your room.' Jonah goes in, and would lock the door, but the lock has no key. Hearing him foolishly fumbling there, the Captain laughs quietly to himself, and mutters something about how the doors of convicts' cells are never allowed to be locked from inside. All dressed and dusty as he is, Jonah throws himself into his berth, and finds the little stateroom's ceiling almost resting on his forehead. The air is close, and Jonah gasps. Then, in that cramped hole, sunk too beneath the ship's waterline, Jonah feels a foreboding, like a herald, of that stifling hour when the whale will hold him in the smallest of the prison wards of his bowels.

items.reason: Opening sentence has a broken absolute construction ('and the ship, heeling over ... , the lamp ... still keeps') that has to be reread, and it slips into past tense ('it only made obvious ... among which it hung') inside present-tense narration.
items.new: "Screwed at its axis against the side, a swinging lamp gently oscillates in Jonah's room; and as the ship heels over toward the wharf with the weight of the last bales taken on, the lamp, flame and all, though slightly moving, still keeps a permanent slant in relation to the room; though in truth, being itself unfailingly straight, it only makes obvious the false, lying levels among which it hangs. The lamp alarms and frightens Jonah; as he lies in his berth his tormented eyes roll around the place, and this so far successful fugitive finds no refuge for his restless glance. But that contradiction in the lamp appalls him more and more. The floor, the ceiling, and the side are all awry. 'Oh! So my conscience hangs in me!' he groans. 'Straight upward it burns; but the chambers of my soul are all in crookedness!'

items.reason: 'grasps a shroud to look out at the sea' — a first-time reader/listener hears 'shroud' as a burial cloth; brief accurate gloss (shrouds are the standing-rigging ropes bracing a mast).
items.new: "And now the time of the tide has come; the ship casts off her cables; and from the deserted wharf the uncheered ship for Tarshish, heeling far over, glides out to sea. That ship, my friends, was the first smuggler on record! The contraband was Jonah. But the sea rebels; it will not bear the wicked burden. A dreadful storm comes on; the ship is about to break up. But now, when the boatswain calls all hands to lighten her; when boxes, bales, and jars are clattering overboard; when the wind is shrieking, and the men are yelling, and every plank thunders with trampling feet right over Jonah's head; in all this raging tumult, Jonah sleeps his hideous sleep. He sees no black sky and raging sea, does not feel the reeling timbers, and little does he hear or heed the distant rush of the mighty whale, which even now, with open mouth, is cleaving the seas after him. Yes, shipmates, Jonah had gone down into the sides of the ship — a berth in the cabin, as I take it — and was fast asleep. But the frightened master comes to him, and shrieks in his dead ear, 'What do you mean, O sleeper? Arise!' Startled from his lethargy by that dreadful cry, Jonah staggers to his feet, and stumbling up to the deck, grasps a shroud, one of the ropes bracing the mast, to look out at the sea. But at that moment a panther of a billow leaps over the bulwarks and springs on him. Wave after wave leaps into the ship like this, and finding no quick way out, runs roaring fore and aft, until the sailors come close to drowning while still afloat. And every time the white moon shows her frightened face from the steep gullies in the blackness overhead, aghast Jonah sees the rearing bowsprit pointing high upward, but soon beaten downward again toward the tormented deep.

items.reason: Tense slip: 'at which the sailors became more and more appalled, but still they pity him' — past 'became' inside present-tense narration.
items.new: "'I am a Hebrew,' he cries — and then — 'I fear the Lord, the God of Heaven, who has made the sea and the dry land!' Fear Him, O Jonah? Yes, well might you fear the Lord God then! Right away he goes on to make a full confession; at which the sailors become more and more appalled, but still they pity him. For when Jonah, not yet begging God for mercy, since he knew all too well the darkness of what he deserved — when wretched Jonah cries out to them to take him and throw him into the sea, for he knew that it was for his sake this great tempest was upon them, they mercifully turn from him, and look for other ways to save the ship. But all in vain; the indignant gale howls louder; then, with one hand raised to God in prayer, with the other they, not without reluctance, lay hold of Jonah.

items.new: We had been sitting hunched like this for some time when all at once I decided to open my eyes. When I'm between sheets, day or night, awake or asleep, I tend to keep my eyes shut to concentrate the snugness of being in bed. Because no person can truly feel their own identity unless their eyes are closed — as if darkness were the proper element of our essence, though light suits our clay better. Opening my eyes and leaving my own pleasant, self-created darkness for the imposed, coarse outer gloom of an unlit midnight, I felt a disagreeable jolt. Nor did I object at all when Queequeg hinted that perhaps we had better light a lamp, since we were wide awake and he badly wanted a few quiet puffs from his tomahawk pipe. I should mention that I'd been dead set against his smoking in bed the night before; yet see how elastic our stiff prejudices become once love starts to bend them. Now I liked nothing better than having Queequeg smoke beside me — even in bed — because he seemed so full of serene, domestic contentment. I no longer worried about the landlord's fire insurance. I was alive only to the condensed, confidential comfort of sharing a pipe and a blanket with a real friend. With our shaggy jackets around our shoulders, we passed the tomahawk pipe back and forth until a blue hanging canopy of smoke slowly gathered above us, glowing in the flame of the newly lit lamp.

items.reason: 'piled on her wharves' directly after 'she glided down the Acushnet' reads as the schooner's wharves; the wharves are New Bedford's.
items.new: At last, with passage paid and luggage safe, we stood on board the schooner. Hoisting sail, she glided down the Acushnet River. On one side, New Bedford rose in terraces of streets, their ice-covered trees all glittering in the clear, cold air. Huge hills and mountains of casks on casks were piled on its wharves, and side by side the world-wandering whale ships lay silent and safely moored at last; while from others came a sound of carpenters and coopers, with the mingled noises of fires and forges to melt the pitch, all signaling that new cruises were starting out; that one most perilous and long voyage ended only begins a second; and a second ended only begins a third, and so on, forever and ever. Such is the endlessness — yes, the intolerableness — of all earthly effort.

items.new: It was quite late in the evening when the little Moss came snugly to anchor and Queequeg and I went ashore; so we could attend to no business that day, at least none but a supper and a bed. The landlord of the Spouter-Inn had recommended us to his cousin Hosea Hussey of the Try Pots, who, he claimed, ran one of the best-kept hotels in all Nantucket; and he had also assured us that Cousin Hosea, as he called him, was famous for his chowders. In short, he plainly hinted that we could not possibly do better than try potluck at the Try Pots. But the directions he had given us — keep a yellow warehouse on our starboard hand till we came in sight of a white church to port, then keep that on the port hand till we made a corner three points to starboard, and that done, ask the first man we met where the place was — these crooked directions of his puzzled us very much at first, especially as, right at the start, Queequeg insisted that the yellow warehouse, our first point of departure, must be left on the port hand, whereas I had understood Peter Coffin to say it was on the starboard. However, by beating about a little in the dark, and now and then knocking at a peaceable inhabitant's door to ask the way, we at last came to something there was no mistaking.
